questions.title: Implement Trie
commonMistakes: Forgetting to mark the end of a full word
Treating prefix search and full-word search as the same operation
Using substring copies that add avoidable overhead
interviewSignals: Defines a small node shape before coding operations
Explains complexity in terms of word length, not number of stored words
followUpPrompts: Add delete support.
Store how many words share each prefix.
Support characters beyond lowercase English letters.
questions.promptSummary: Design a prefix tree that supports inserting words, full-word lookup, and prefix lookup.
questions.highLevelApproach: Represent each character as an edge to a child node and mark nodes that complete a word; each operation walks the characters of the input string once.
questions.problemStatement: Implement a Trie (prefix tree) with insert, search, and startsWith operations. insert adds a word, search returns whether a complete word was previously inserted, and startsWith returns whether any inserted word begins with a given prefix.
constraints: word and prefix consist of lowercase English letters.
At most 3 * 10^4 calls are made to insert, search, and startsWith.

examples.input: Trie trie = new Trie(); trie.insert("apple"); trie.search("apple"); trie.search("app"); trie.startsWith("app"); trie.insert("app"); trie.search("app")
examples.explanation: apple is a complete word, app is initially only a prefix, and becomes searchable after it is inserted.
No inserted word begins with the prefix car.

questions.keyInsight: The key is to recognize the prefix tree pattern and maintain the right invariant around prefix tree nodes. Once that invariant is clear, the implementation is mostly careful state updates.
hints: Start with the most direct brute-force idea and say why it is too slow or too memory-heavy.
Look for the prefix tree structure: what state can be carried forward instead of recomputed?
Be careful about this common trap: Forgetting to mark the end of a full word.
The intended path is: Represent each character as an edge to a child node and mark nodes that complete a word; each operation walks the characters of the input string once.

approaches.name: Baseline — direct search or simulation
approaches.idea: Use the straightforward interpretation of the prompt first. This is useful in an interview because it proves you understand the task before optimizing.
steps: Restate what each candidate answer would need to check.
Try every relevant candidate or simulate the process directly.
Compare the result with the required output and identify repeated work.
approaches.tradeoff: Good for explaining the problem, but usually misses the target complexity and should be improved before finalizing.

approaches.name: Intended — prefix tree
approaches.idea: Represent each character as an edge to a child node and mark nodes that complete a word; each operation walks the characters of the input string once.
steps: Track the state needed for prefix tree nodes.
Update that state in a single disciplined pass, traversal, or recursive branch.
Preserve the invariant after every update and return the value the prompt asks for.
approaches.tradeoff: This is the interview-ready approach: it connects the recognizable pattern to the expected complexity.

questions.title: Design Add and Search Words Data Structure
commonMistakes: Trying to handle '.' with a single child lookup
Returning true for prefixes that are not complete words
Ignoring worst-case branching when many wildcards appear
interviewSignals: Reuses trie design cleanly and adds DFS only for wildcard positions
Calls out the exponential worst case but efficient normal-case lookup
followUpPrompts: Support '*' matching zero or more characters.
Return all matching words instead of a boolean.

questions.promptSummary: Design a word dictionary that supports adding words and searching with '.' as any one character.
questions.highLevelApproach: Insert words into a trie. For search, recurse through exact characters normally and branch over all children when the pattern contains a wildcard.

complexity.time: O(L) average, O(26^W * L) worst case with W wildcards

questions.problemStatement: Design a WordDictionary that supports addWord and search. The search pattern may contain lowercase letters and '.'; a dot matches any single letter.
constraints: word consists of lowercase English letters.
search patterns contain lowercase English letters and '.', with at most 2 dots.
At most 10^4 calls are made to addWord and search.

examples.input: WordDictionary dict = new WordDictionary(); dict.addWord("bad"); dict.addWord("dad"); dict.addWord("mad"); dict.search("pad"); dict.search("bad"); dict.search(".ad"); dict.search("b..")
examples.explanation: pad was not inserted, while bad matches directly, .ad matches dad or mad, and b.. matches bad.
The wildcard matches the single inserted character a, but b does not.

questions.title: Subsets

Generate subsets iteratively.

questions.promptSummary: Return every subset of a list of distinct integers.
questions.highLevelApproach: Backtrack through the array, either including or skipping each value, copying the current path whenever a complete decision path is reached.
questions.problemStatement: Given an array nums of distinct integers, return all possible subsets (the power set). The answer must not contain duplicate subsets, and the order of subsets does not matter.
constraints: All values in nums are unique.

examples.explanation: Each number is independently included or excluded, producing 2^3 = 8 subsets.
The empty subset and the subset containing 0 are the only possibilities.

questions.title: Combination Sum
commonMistakes: Generating the same combination in different orders
Advancing the start index when reuse of the same number is still allowed
Missing the overshoot pruning condition
interviewSignals: Uses a start index to keep combinations ordered
Explains when recursion may stay on the same index versus move forward
followUpPrompts: Disallow reusing each candidate.
Handle duplicate candidate values.
Count combinations without listing them.
questions.promptSummary: Find all unique combinations of candidate numbers that sum to a target, allowing repeated use of each candidate.
questions.highLevelApproach: Sort or iterate candidates in a fixed order, backtrack with a remaining target, and pass the current index again when choosing a reusable candidate.

complexity.time: O(N^(T/M)) in the rough worst case

questions.problemStatement: Given an array of distinct positive integers candidates and a target integer target, return all unique combinations of candidates that sum to target. Each candidate may be chosen unlimited times, and the order of combinations does not matter.

examples.explanation: The two unique combinations that sum to 7 are 2+2+3 and 7.
Each listed combination uses candidates repeatedly and totals 8.

questions.title: Word Search II

interviewSignals: Builds a trie from all words before touching the board
Prunes DFS as soon as the current prefix is absent
followUpPrompts: Remove found words from the trie to prune future searches.

questions.promptSummary: Find all dictionary words that can be formed by walking adjacent cells on a character board.
questions.highLevelApproach: Insert all words into a trie, then start DFS from each board cell while following trie edges; mark cells visited for the active path and record words when terminal nodes are reached.

complexity.time: O(m*n*4^L) worst case, heavily pruned by trie prefixes

examples.explanation: eat and oath can be traced through adjacent unused cells; pea and rain cannot.
The word would require reusing the b cell, which is not allowed.

questions.title: N-Queens
commonMistakes: Checking the full board for conflicts every time without using constraint sets
Computing diagonal identifiers incorrectly
Forgetting to remove column or diagonal state during backtracking
interviewSignals: Uses columns and both diagonal sets for O(1) conflict checks

followUpPrompts: Return only the number of valid boards.

questions.promptSummary: Place n queens on an n x n board so no two attack each other, returning all valid boards.
questions.highLevelApproach: Place queens one row at a time, skipping columns or diagonals already occupied, and roll back those constraint sets after each recursive branch.
questions.problemStatement: Place n queens on an n x n chessboard so that no two queens attack each other. Return all distinct valid board configurations, using 'Q' for a queen and '.' for an empty square.

examples.explanation: The two listed boards are the only arrangements where no queens share a row, column, or diagonal.
A one-cell board has one valid placement.

questions.keyInsight: The key is to recognize the recursive search with pruning pattern and maintain the right invariant around row-by-row placement. Once that invariant is clear, the implementation is mostly careful state updates.

Look for the recursive search with pruning structure: what state can be carried forward instead of recomputed?
